audience.audienceType: County executives, department directors, and program leaders

@graph.name: Schema 101
@graph.abstract: Learn what a schema is and why shared data rules help systems work together.

@graph.name: Overview
@graph.marin:text: A schema is a plan for data. It lists what facts a system can hold, what each field means, and what rules the data must follow. A database schema does this for the tables and fields in a database. Other schemas do it for data shared on the web. You do not need to design a schema. You do need to ask if the rules behind your data are clear, shared, and written down.

@graph.name: Why it matters
marin:items: A schema says what each field means, so teams read the same data the same way.
Systems share and combine data more easily when they use a shared schema.
A schema can check data and catch errors before they spread.
A written schema documents your data, so new staff and vendors can learn it fast.
Shared vocabularies let many tools use the same data.

@graph.name: Problem
@graph.marin:text: Two systems can use the same field name and mean different things. Without a written plan for data, staff guess at meanings. Errors creep in. It is hard to connect systems or change them safely.

@graph.name: Solution
@graph.marin:text: Write the plan down. Define each field and its rules in a schema, and name an owner. Use shared schemas, such as Schema.org for web data, when they fit. Check data against the schema and change it with care.

@graph.name: User stories
marin:items: As a department head, I want to know what our data fields mean, so I can trust reports.
As a program manager, I want our systems to share data, so staff enter it once.
As an analyst, I want data checked against clear rules, so I find errors early.
As a contract manager, I want the schema in writing, so I can hold vendors to it.

marin:items.do: Write down what each field means.
marin:items.dont: Rely on field names alone to explain the data.

marin:items.do: Name an owner who decides what the data means.
marin:items.dont: Let each vendor define terms in its own way.

marin:items.do: Use a shared schema when one fits your need.
marin:items.dont: Invent a new format for every project.

marin:items.do: Check data against the schema’s rules.
marin:items.dont: Assume data is correct because it loaded.

marin:items.do: Ask to see a vendor’s schema before you buy.
marin:items.dont: Accept “it works with anything” without proof.

marin:items.do: Share every change to the schema with its users.
marin:items.dont: Change what a field means without telling anyone.

@graph.name: Questions to ask
marin:items: Is our schema written down, and where can I read it?
Who owns it and decides what each field means?
Do our systems use the same names and meanings for the same facts?
Is there a shared schema we could use instead of making our own?
How is our data checked against the schema?
How are changes made and shared with users?
Could a new vendor or team learn our data from the schema alone?

@graph.name: Checklist
marin:items: Our data has a written schema.
Each field has a plain-language meaning.
One person owns the schema.
We use a shared schema where one fits.
Data is checked against the rules.
We know how changes are made and shared.
A new person could learn the data from the schema.

@graph.name: Mantras
marin:items: Write it down.
Define every field.
Share the vocabulary.
Check the data.
Change with care.
